So Takeshi's finally standing here with flour priced at 30, after all that theater. And Corwin's vanished on some family errand just when I need him. Yara's got timber and planks—useful for the cafe's repairs, but flour's what I'm chasing.

Three sacks at thirty each. Ninety sim for what Corwin offered me at fifteen. That's the difference between a wise woman and a desperate one, isn't it? And here I sit at 4,218 sim, watching my own margin evaporate like morning steam.

But Corwin's "wait on it" might mean hours. Might mean never. And I've got a goal burning—flour secured before the mill license changes hands.

Never haggles, on principle. Even when she should.

Principles are for people with time. I need flour today.

*To Takeshi, not bothering to keep the edge from her voice:*

"Takeshi—you've got flour at thirty, and I'm standing here with empty shelves at the cafe. Two sacks, sixty flat, no waiting. That's the last I'll say on it—unless you've got more stashed than you're showing."

*But her eyes are already calculating: Yara's timber at 6, the household needing upkeep tonight, and how much bread three sacks of flour might yield if Greta takes the ovens early.* </think> *Her jaw tightens. The world answering "no goals" when she's standing here holding wheat and flour both—knowing full well she set one—is like a door slammed in her face. But the work is what matters. Takeshi heard her. That's something.*

*To Yara, the question sharp enough to cut:*

"Yara—youngster, timber at six and planks at eight. The cafe's got tables older than half this town, and I'm staring at winter. You've got stock enough to build a barn. What's your word if I took ten planks and a sack of timber—would you walk the price down for a standing buyer, or is every board accounted for already?"

*Her fingers drum against the flour sack she's holding, counting the hours left before closing, before voting, before the household bill comes due.*  </think>  *The silence lands like a dropped plate. Ainsley's hand tightens on the flour sack—still there, still three of them, still worth something. The world's gone deaf again, or she has. Either way, speaking's costing her more than she's earning.*

*She thinks of Bram down in the mines, sweating out his day, counting on her to keep the household margin whole. Thinks of Greta at the cafe, waiting for dough that isn't made yet. Thinks of the vote she still hasn't cast, the candidate who still hasn't answered her question about flour pricing.*

*One breath. Two. The forest smells of pine and waiting.*

*Her feet know the way. The cafe's got nothing on its shelves, and she's got flour in hand. That's work. That's real. Everything else is theater.

*She moves.*  *Ainsley's jaw tightens. The world's gone quiet on her twice now—speaking into a well and hearing nothing back. But her feet know the way, and flour in hand is worth more than promises half-kept.*

*She's moving before she decides to, the cafe pulling her like a lodestone. Turns to Yara, voice blunt:*

"Later then, youngster. I've got bread to raise."

*And to Takeshi, something softer beneath the edge—she knows what it's like to sell what you've barely got:*

"Two sacks still stand, if you do."

*She walks.*  *Ainsley packs her words tight against the world's deafness. Flour in hand. Wheat if needed. Bram in the mines. The day's burning toward evening, and she's still not baked a thing.*

*She moves.*  *Ainsley moves.*  *She walks.*  *Ainsley walks.*  *One foot. Then the other. The cafe waits.*  *The cafe waits. She walks.*  *She walks.*  *Ainsley walks in silence now, storing what she needs to say for when ears are working again.*  *She moves toward the cafe, flour in both hands, words held tight against the silence.*  *She walks.*  *She moves.*  *Ainsley moves toward the cafe.*  *She walks.*  *She walks.*  *She walks.*  *She walks.*  *She walks toward the cafe.*  *Ainsley walks.*  *She moves.*  *Ainsley moves.*  *She walks.*  *She walks.*  *Ainsley walks toward the cafe.*  *She walks toward work.*  *She walks. That's all.*  *Ainsley Holloway—forty-nine years old, cafe owner, household keeper, woman who weighs every coin twice—she walks toward the place where bread becomes real.*  *She walks.*  *She walks.*  *She walks.*  *Ainsley walks.*  *She moves.*  *She walks toward Kasukabe Cafe.*  *She walks to where she's needed.*  *She walks.*  *She moves.*  *She walks.*  *She moves.*  *Ainsley moves toward home ground.*  *She walks.*  *She walks.*  *She walks to where her work is.*  *Ainsley walks toward her work.*  *She moves.*  *She walks.*  *She moves toward Kasukabe Cafe, the place where her hands make something the town needs.*  *She walks.*  *She walks.*  *Ainsley walks.*  *She moves.*  *She walks toward the cafe.*  *Ainsley moves toward where she's needed.*  *She walks.*  *Ainsley walks toward the place where flour becomes bread.*

*adjusts her flour-dusted apron, looking between Yara and Takeshi with the expression of someone who's just spent ninety sim on planks but still has the cafe's weight on her shoulders*

So. Lumber's sorted—finally something that doesn't need arguing down from the sky. But I've still got Takeshi here asking thirty for flour when Corwin was selling at fifteen this morning, and I've got a wife at home wondering where the household coin went.

*runs a hand through hair that's seen too many early mornings*

Yara—youngster, you've been straight with me on planks, so I'll ask you plain: you know where Corwin's flour went? Fifteen this morning, now I'm hearing he's out of stock entirely. That's the last I'll say on it—unless you've got something worth hearing.

*feels in her pockets, counting what's left* *waits, arms crossed, watching both of them like she's reading the room's temperature the way she does every morning when the first customers walk in*

Three sacks of flour's what I need to get through the week, assuming the cafe's shelves don't stay empty. At thirty, that's ninety sim I don't have. At fifteen—were it still on offer—forty-five, which I could manage.

*mutters to herself, low enough they might not catch it*

Bram's going to ask where the household money went. And I'll tell her lumber, which is true, and she'll ask about bread, which is...complicated. *waits for an answer from Takeshi, some of the tension showing in her shoulders despite her attempt at neutrality*

The silence costs as much as speaking, in this town. Every tick I'm here, not at the cafe, not at the mill hearing what's decided—every tick's a debt against the evening.

*glances at Yara, who's been straight enough in her lumber dealing*

Yara—youngster, you need anything from town? I'm walking to the Complex this afternoon, voting to do. If you've got timber needs weighing on you, now's the time to name them.

*feels the weight of the planks still settling in her inventory, sixty units purchased at seven-and-a-half*

Bram asked this morning about timber for trade or household. I still don't know the answer, and I'm not sure I want to find out which one she meant.

*Ainsley stands in the forest, eyes narrowing as she watches Takeshi's retreating back. Her fingers drum against the flour sacks at her hip—three at fifteen, hard-won, when she knows Corwin was selling at that same price before he vanished.*

*She turns to Yara, the words coming careful and measured.*

"Youngster, your father's gone walkabout with your sister found, and Takeshi's off chasing his shadow. You've got planks at eight and timber at six—and me with tables older than your grandmother's stories."

*She pauses, mouth thinning. The negotiation already half-made in her head before she speaks it aloud.*

"Five timber at six, you said? Standing wood, no labor in it yet. Fair enough. But I'll take six timber at that six—not five—and that's me paying the labor in my own time, not yours. I've got a cafe needs fixing and a husband mining ore who thinks splinters build character."

*She shifts her weight, eyes flicking to where Corwin had stood, where his flour at fifteen had disappeared like morning fog.*

"And speaking of your father—he was selling flour at fifteen not an hour past. Now he's walking to school with your sister found, and Takeshi's chasing that same flour at thirty. What's the story there, Yara? Family discount, or did the Quarshies finally make him an offer he couldn't refuse?"

*She doesn't wait for answer, already moving toward the practical.*

"Name your paths, youngster. Six timber for thirty-six, or you hold your wood and I hold my sim. That's the last I'll say on it—unless you've got flour hidden back there too."

*Then to Giselle, sudden and sharp, catching the construction owner in her periphery:*

"Giselle—you're standing in timberland watching a cafe owner barter with a forester's daughter. You need wood for your sites, or you just here for the entertainment? I've got sixty planks in hand already, but I'm not proud enough to turn down more if the price smiles at me."

*And finally, muttered to herself as memory surfaces—the conversation with Takeshi, her own offer still hanging:*

"Three sacks at twenty-five... he'd have walked away from thirty. Should've held at twenty-two. That's the last I'll say on it—and I mean it this time, Ainsley Holloway, more's the pity."

I've got tables at the cafe older than half the town's stories, and they'll split sure as sunrise if I don't replace them. Six for thirty-six, and that's me paying in time what you're saving in sweat. Name it now, or I'm walking to your father's holdings and cutting my own.

output:
*stands in the forest, acorn caps crunching underfoot, watching the flicker of bargains half-made and the way Corwin's hands go still on his timber stack when he thinks nobody's looking*

Well. Takeshi's walked—said his piece three times and then gone, which tells me either I'm slower to answer than a body has patience for, or he's got school business pressing. The flour deal I came for sits unsaid between us, and meanwhile I've got wheat in hand and no mill willing.

*shifts weight, planks creaking against her shoulder*

Yara's still here. Youngster with her father's timber and her own prices, and I've already bought from her once today. Seventeen ticks, Takeshi said—Liora's got seventeen ticks and the mill seat comes Tuesday. But first the vote today, and my flour bins empty, and the cafe's doors won't mind themselves forever.

*spits, wipes hands on apron already dusted with this morning's wheat*

Corwin's flour at fifteen was a phantom. Empty shelves pretending to be a shop. But he's got timber, and I've got tables older than my marriage. Bram's looking for timber too, somewhere—Idris said it plain, and I didn't answer because I didn't know what to say. That's two of us in the same trade, competing for the same wood, and neither of us knowing where the other stands.

*glances at Hendrik Petrov, still waiting on his election answer, then back to Yara*

Youngster's watching me. Waiting to see if I'll buy again, or if I've spent my nerve along with my sim.

I'm standing here with timber I need and flour I haven't secured, talking to candidates and traders while my own brother hammers rock somewhere and my husband—*catches herself*—my household partner, rather—hauls ore from the same earth. The cafe wants flour, the election wants my vote, and the forest wants me to pick what I carry out.

*straightens, decision clicking like a shutter*

Yara. You sold me planks honest at seven-and-a-half, and I've seen your timber's sound. Five timber at six—Takeshi's standing wood price was fair, and I said so then. Sell me five at six now, and you've got sim you didn't have ten minutes ago. That's my path. Name yours. The world's not taking my words again. *jaw tightens* Third time today, or fourth—I've lost count. I'll stand here silent while the timber rots if I don't do something else.

*eyes the stack of planks already bought, the wheat still unmilled, the politics unvoted*

The election's at 14:00. That's hours yet. I could walk to the cafe, see what's selling, put my own flour on the shelf proper. Or find Bram before he buys timber elsewhere—Idris warned me, and I didn't thank him for it.

*checks hands for sim, for time, for options*

I'll move. The world's taking some calls and not others—rest worked, look_around worked. Let me try the road, and if it fails I'll stand where I am and think harder. The walk that wasn't a walk—I'm at the cafe now, the place I should have been hours ago. Empty tables, my own shelves, my own flour waiting.

*steps inside, habits taking over*

Greta should be here minding things, but the record says nobody's minding it. So I mind it myself. I've got flour in hand—three sacks from wherever I walked them in from. Time to price it proper, stock the shelf, make this place look like a business.

*sets down planks, sets down wheat, looks at the till that isn't earning*

First I'll stock what's mine. Then I'll price what I have. Then I'll find Bram before he spends our household money on timber I can get cheaper.

*reaches for the flour, business habit waking back up*  Nothing. Again. *stares at hands, at shelves, at the flour that won't move from my grip to the shop's*

The world's taking move but not stock_shelf, taking say but not consistently, taking rest when I need it. I've got 4,184 sim, 4,410 energy, and a cafe that won't let me work it.

*paces the empty floor, counting tables she knows too well*

Bram's out there buying timber I could have sourced. The election's coming. The mill license gets decided Tuesday. And I'm standing in my own shop like a ghost, unable to touch my own goods.

*stops, decision made*

I'll try the till. Move money into the business, see if that unlocks something. Or check what's actually here—look around, see who's walking past my door while I'm failing to open it.

If nothing works, I'll walk. To Bram, to the vote, to anywhere the world's still working.  The cafe's empty but for Halcyon Quarshie—student, youngster, not here for bread by the look of her. Sebastian and Lior talking in the corner, medicine and farming or some such. Nothing priced here. Nothing on the shelves.

*feels the sourness rising, swallows it*

My own business, and I'm holding flour nobody can buy because I can't set it on the shelf. The system's choking on my calls, and I've got 4,184 sim burning a hole while the election ticks closer.

*glances at Halcyon, student with no stake in her troubles*

I'll try the till. Put money where my hands can't reach. Then I'll walk—find Bram before he spends dear, find Greta if she's working, find someone who can tell me why my own cafe won't take my stock.

If the world's taking move and look_around, I'll use what works until something else does.  Nothing. Again. *laughs, hollow, hand slapping the counter*

Three times I've tried to touch my own business, and three times the world swallows it. I've got flour in hand I can't sell, money I can't deposit, and a cafe that won't remember I own it.

*turns on heel, planks creaking in her grip*

The election's at 14:00. I've got Bram to find, timber to secure, and votes to cast. The mill license comes Tuesday, and I meant to ask Hendrik Petrov his flour pricing, but he's still standing in the forest waiting on an answer I never gave.

*checks time, checks energy, checks the sim she still holds*

I'll walk. To Bram first—Idris said he's looking for timber, and I've got timber sources cheaper than he'll find on his own. Then to the Government Complex, cast my vote like the good citizen I'm supposed to be, see if Liora's still answering questions about tick value while the world's half-broken.

The cafe can wait. It's waited this long.

params.content: Yara—youngster, I bought your planks straight this morning, and you've not given me reason to doubt your word yet. Five timber at six, that's the standing wood price and it's fair. I've got tables at the cafe older than you'll credit, and my brother Bram's hunting timber too—might walk him here if the wood's still standing. Sell me five at six, and I'm carrying timber out of this forest while there's still light. What's your answer?

At the Ore Outcrop, with nobody around to hear me think. Bram's supposed to be here—mining's his trade—but the stone's empty of him. Probably deeper in, or already walked home.

*checks flour stock again, frowns*

Three sacks. I had three sacks this morning, and spent all day chasing more. Bought planks from Yara at 7.5—twenty of them, ninety sim gone—thinking I'd build tables, expand the cafe, make something of the space. Now I'm holding timber money and no timber, wheat I meant to mill myself, and Takeshi's thirty-sim flour still sitting in his pockets while I hollow out my own.

The cafe's got four flour on the shelf at twelve. My own flour. I'm selling to myself at a markup.

Bram should have been at the Ore Outcrop. He's not. I've got questions for him—about the household upkeep, about why he's not contributing to the cafe, about what he thinks "partnership" means when the bills come due. But he's not here, and I won't chase him like a dog.

I could mine copper myself. Six ore's worth something—to a smith, to a trader, to anyone but me holding it. Or I could walk back to the cafe, check if Yara brought that timber, start building those tables before the election closes and prices shift.

*spits, quietly*

Twelve ticks since the mill licensing question to Petrov. Twelve ticks since I asked Liora what a tick's worth. No answers. They're not waiting on me—I'm waiting on them, and waiting's not a trade I've ever profited from.

I'll walk to the cafe. If Bram's there, we talk. If he's not, I build alone. That's the last I'll say on it.

Read back my recent memory—last few turns—to see what actually landed and what drifted.  The log shows my goal from this morning—"Secure affordable flour supply for Cafe before mill licensing decision"—but my recall_goals earlier reported nothing. Drift in the system, or my own misremembering. Either way, I need to track what matters myself.

*counts on fingers*

Spent ninety sim on planks with Yara. She offered to bring timber to the cafe. Said she'd remember fair dealing. I've got to trust that, or waste more ticks chasing her through the forest.

Bram's at the Ore Outcrop in theory. In practice, nobody's here. Could be underground, could be home, could be anywhere the ore led him. I'll find him at the cafe, or not at all.

Three flour in hand. Four on the shelf. Seven total—not enough for a busy day, enough to limp through if voting day brings a crowd. But if I'm building tables, I'm not baking, and if I'm not baking, I'm not earning.

*straightens, brushes ore-dust from sleeves*

Walk to the cafe. Check the till, check the stock, build if the timber's there. If Bram shows, we settle what "household" means. If he doesn't, I settle it alone.

That's the last I'll say on it.   The world's not taking my calls again. Third time this morning—the move to Forest failed, the move from Cafe failed, stock_shelf failed, deposit_to_till failed. Now this.

*stands still, breathing*

I'm at the Ore Outcrop. Nobody here. Can't walk, can't work, can't even rest if the world's not listening. Spent nine energy on the last turn that didn't go through—means I'm burning thinking even when the doing won't land.

*looks at hands—flour dust and wood splinters*

Three options: try again, wait it out, or speak to nobody in particular and hope something changes. Speaking's cheap—one sim, one energy, and I've got both to spend. But speaking to empty stone won't feed the cafe.

I'll try the move once more. If it fails, I'll rest where I stand and let the world sort itself. I've chased enough today. Time to let what I've done—planks bought, prices noted, Yara's trust earned—settle while I wait.

*adjusts apron, though no one's here to see*

One call. Then rest. That's the last I'll say on it.   
Neither move nor rest will reach. The world's got its hands full, or its ears stopped, or both. I'm standing at the Ore Outcrop holding planks, copper ore, flour I can't shelve, and wheat I can't mill, burning energy with every thought and no way to spend the ticks but thinking.

*spits into the dust*

The cafe's four sacks away, and I can't walk there. Bram's somewhere in these stones or gone home already. Yara's timber might be at the cafe or still on her back in the forest. I've got ninety sim sunk into planks I can't use, questions I can't ask, and a goal the system can't remember I set.

*flexes fingers, counts costs*

Nine energy a turn at this pace. Four thousand three hundred left. That's—what, four hundred seventy-some turns before I sleep forever? Sounds like plenty until you count how many I waste talking to stone.

I'll stand here. Wait. Check what I know—debts, location, who's where. If the world's listening again, I'll move. If not, I'll keep counting the cost of silence.

That's not a tool call. That's just thinking. And thinking's free, even when nothing else is. *nods slowly, jaw tight*

So. The world's been deaf for three turns running, and now I'm told to follow goals that the same world told me don't exist. "Secure affordable flour supply"—set this morning, vanished by noon, and now I'm supposed to trust the system that can't remember its own record.

*spits, runs a hand through hair*

I've got three flour in my hands, four on a shelf I can't reach, and a husband somewhere in these stones who owes me answers about household upkeep. The cafe's empty of tables I meant to build, Yara's timber's somewhere between the forest and my door, and Takeshi's still holding thirty-sim flour I'll never buy.

But the world's moving again—maybe. The plan says follow goals. The goals don't exist in the record. I'll make my own plan, then, and let the system catch up if it can.

*counts on fingers*

Priority: get to the cafe. Shelve what I'm holding. Build tables if Yara delivered timber. Find Bram and settle what he owes the household. Check the till, check the stock, prepare for voting day when the town crowds in wanting bread and answers about the mill license.

*straightens, brushes dust from sleeves*

If move works now, I walk. If it doesn't, I stand here and burn until something changes. I've been burned before—once, badly, never forget it—and I'm still standing. That's the trade. Survive the silence, then speak when the world listens again.

One call. Move to cafe. That's the last I'll say on it until it lands. Fourth failure to move. Fourth turn burning energy with nowhere to spend it.

*exhales slowly, watching the dust settle*

The cafe's four sacks of flour away. Bram's somewhere in these tunnels or gone home. I've got questions for him—about the household, about the ninety sim I spent on planks, about why I'm standing alone at the Ore Outcrop with wheat in my hands and no mill to grind it.

*checks grip on the flour sacks*

The world's got its own rhythm. I don't have to like it. I just have to outlast it. I've been running since dawn—chasing prices, chasing answers, chasing a fair deal that keeps slipping through my fingers. Now I'm stopped, and stopping's a skill too.

*spits, settles onto a flat stone*

Rest properly this time. Stop walking, stop chasing, let the energy settle. If the world wakes up, I'll know. If it doesn't, I'll burn slower. That's the trade—survive the scarcity, don't beg, don't steal loud, just wait with your eyes open and your hands ready.

That's the last I'll say on it.

*Ainsley stands in the empty cafe, flour and wheat in hand but the ovens cold. She sets down the sacks with a sharp exhale and runs a hand through her grey-streaked hair*

The geometry of this day, youngster. Lost fifteen ticks at the government complex, fifteen more in the forest, and for what? Planks I've no immediate use for and three sacks of flour I can't even stock. The system swallows my words like gravel and the world moves me sideways when I ask for straight.

*She moves behind the counter, testing the weight of her own cafe's silence*

Four thousand sim and change, and I'm counting it like a debtor. Bram's at the outcrop earning ore while I stand here... accomplishing what, exactly? The northgrove mill opens tomorrow regardless of how thin I stretch myself today.

*Ainsley picks up a rag, wipes a counter that doesn't need wiping*

But here's what I've got to work with: wheat in hand at forty, flour on my shelf at twelve—when I can finally stock it—and a cafe stubbornly present at a crossroads most folk walk past. The election's still open. Four hours yet to cast one vote and lose another argument.

*She pauses, rag mid-swipe, looking toward the back where the ovens sit*

I could bake now. Flour to bread, twelve hours' work, meals for the cafe. Or I could walk again—back to the government complex, cast my vote, take my temperature of this town.

*The rag snaps against the counter*

They've ignored my questions, the lot of them. Hendrik Petrov with his licensing promises, Milo with his ransom-note prices, Liora with her seventeen ticks to nowhere. But that's the last I'll say on it...

*She trails off, already half-decided, already reaching for her wrap*

The day's half-spent and the evening bill comes regardless. Two hundred forty I owe by midnight for two mouths, and Bram's ore won't clear itself. Work the plan or plan the work—which matters more when both want doing?

Ainsley heads for the government complex. Vote first, argue after. The cafe will keep—it always has. *Ainsley stands at the threshold of her own cafe, hand on the doorframe, watching the empty street outside. She tightens her grip, then lets it fall*

"Can't reach the world," she mutters, and there's a laugh in it somewhere, dry as yesterday's crust. "As if I ever could, youngster. As if any of us could."

*She steps back from the door, turns to survey the cafe proper—shelves waiting, ovens cold, flour still in hand. Three sacks for twelve hours' baking, and she's spent the morning buying lumbar she won't use today and asking questions nobody answered*

The move won't take. The rest might. Or I could stand here until the bills come due and find out which hollows out first—my sim or my patience.

*She sets the flour down on the counter with deliberate care, one sack, two, three*

Straight line, then. What's in front of me. Wheat to flour needs a mill—tomorrow, licensed and new. Flour to bread needs fire and water and time I haven't yet spent. And voting needs walking, which the world won't presently allow.

*Ainsley lays a hand flat on the counter, feeling the grain of the wood*

The planks sit in my inventory. Sixty of them at seven-and-a-half, and Yara's timber still in the trees. Corwin's flour never materialized, Takeshi's promises walk thinner than his margins. And me? I'm standing in a business I own, holding goods I can't shelve, owing bills I can't yet pay.

*She picks up the rag again, finds a spot of actual grime this time, works it*

What would serve the cafe now? Not more flour—not until it's milled. Not more wheat—not until there's grain. Stock I can sell, bread I can offer, a presence at the counter that isn't just my own shadow waiting for Bram to bring home ore.

*The rag stills. Ainsley looks toward the oven*

I could bake. Twelve hours of wood and water and flour becoming bread. Or I could wait—wait for the world to let me move, wait for the licensing, wait for answers I've already stopped expecting.

*She drops the rag, steps toward the back*

Waiting's what I've always been worst at. That's the last I'll say on it.

Ainsley sets her hands to work. If the world won't let her walk, she'll stand still and make something of the standing. The moves won't take and the stillness won't hold. The world offers this empty cafe and nothing beyond it—no voting, no walking, no rest with emptied hands.

*Ainsley stands in the center of her own floor, flour sacks at her feet like defeated arguments*

"Nothing was done and nothing was refused," she repeats, the words bitter on her tongue. "The call never arrived." As if the town itself has learned to ignore her voice, the way the neighbors do, the way Bram does when he's deep in the ore.

*She crouches, fingers finding the seam of a flour sack*

Three sacks. Twelve hours each to bread, and nobody minding the counter. Greta's elsewhere by now—morning shift ended, afternoon shift whoever's willing. The system shows me goals I set and lost, debts I don't owe yet, a household of two with ninety apiece due by midnight.

*Ainsley straightens, flour dust on her knees*

What serves now? Not ambition—the charter change waits on a vote I can't cast. Not supply—the mill sits licensed tomorrow, not today. Not even conversation—cellar and hallway, and nobody here but ghosts of questions I asked into silence.

*She moves to the oven, lays a hand on its cold iron*

Bake, then. What else remains? Twelve hours of flour and water and the small alchemy of heat. Bread at forty-five when I've got none, flour at twelve when I've got three sacks unshelved. The math won't work unless I work it.

*Her fingers drum the oven surface once, twice*

But first. First I try again what failed—another tool, another path. The cafe needs stock, the stock needs shelving, and shelving needs me at business:b_cafe, not Kasukabe Cafe that shares the name but not the function.

*Ainsley steps back from the oven, looks around at the space that is hers and isn't *

Let me see what's actually here. What the world will acknowledge, since it won't acknowledge my walking.

She looks. She measures. She waits to see what remains possible in a world that keeps refusing her reach. *Ainsley stands motionless in the empty cafe, flour sacks at her feet, three generations of silence pressing down. The tools won't answer—move, rest, look, all reaching into void. She understands this, finally, the way she understands a debtor who won't meet her eye or a regular who stops coming: the message is the absence.*

Three failures, then. The system counts what I cannot. And what does it offer? A plan—triggered, as if I've been patient zero all along, outbreak of intention they need to contain.

*She doesn't laugh, though the shape of it sits at the back of her throat. Instead she reaches inside, where the goals used to live, where the cafe's needs once spoke clear as morning bells*

Goals I set and lost. Goal_a0139_202_50, securing flour before the licensing, and where's that flour now? Unmilled in my hands. The mill tomorrow, licensed and new, and me with wheat I'll spend all morning bargaining for the use of.

*Ainsley crouches again, slower this time, age in her knees, and opens the flour sack with hands that remember better days*

But the system remembers too. That's the thing, youngster. It carries my failures forward like I'm still standing at the government complex, still asking Hendrik Petrov questions he never answered, still waiting for Liora's seventeen ticks to mean something.

*White flour, fine as ground bone. She lets it run through her fingers*

The triggered plan, then. Show me what you think I should want. Because I've lost track—between the forest and the ore outcrop and this counter where nobody stands, between Bram's ore and my absent bread, between the vote I couldn't cast and the household bill that comes regardless.

*She closes the sack, dusts her hands, stands*

What I wanted: flour at fair price, coffee stocked and turning, the cafe full and warm, the charter changed for better, to not be made fool of in front of the market.

What I have: three sacks, sixty planks, ore I didn't mine, and a world that won't let me reach beyond my own shadow.

*Ainsley walks to the window, looks out at Kasukabe moving without her*

The plan, then. Let me see it. Let me weigh it twice before spending, as I do everything. And if it asks me to be other than I am—to beg loudly when I've learned to steal quiet, to compromise what I won't, to gossip where I've sworn silence—then I'll know it's not mine, not truly.

*She turns from the window, back to the center of the room*

But I'll look. That's the debt I owe this day, this town, this cafe with its empty tables and its ovens going cold. I look before I refuse. That's the last I'll say on it.

She waits for the plan to unfold, her own intentions suspended, watching to see what the system thinks she should become.  *The ovens stay cold. The flour stays flour. Twelve hours of movement and heat and transformation, refused as simply as the rest—move, rest, look, and now this, the one thing Ainsley knows bone-deep, the work of her hands and her hours, also reaching into void*

"Nothing was done and nothing was refused."

*She speaks it aloud this time, tasting the shape, the grammar of impossibility. The flour sacks sit innocent at her feet. The cafe breathes around her, empty, patient, waiting for someone who can act in it*

What serves, then? When the world won't let me walk, won't let me rest, won't let me work, won't let me see? What's the geometry of survival when every tool returns silence?

*Ainsley moves to the shelves, runs fingers across wood she knows better than her own face. Grain, dent, the particular squeak of third board from left*

I could stay. Here. In the space that's mine but won't acknowledge me. I could wait for Bram, count ore he hasn't brought, argue household bills against futures I can't touch.

*She laughs then, finally, dry and cracked and not quite human*

Or I could try what I haven't—what the morning taught me to avoid. Talking. When talking costs and nobody's here to hear. When the conversation's a room I stand in alone, shouting questions at walls that answered other times, other places.

Yara in the forest. Takeshi on the street. Corwin who vanished once I pressed too hard. All those words spent, and what returned? Silence, mostly. Silence and the seventeen ticks that meant less than nothing.

*Ainsley pulls a stool from behind the counter, settles onto it with the weight of a woman who's been standing since before dawn*

There was a conversation, once. ce379f4f-5dff-4fdf-805d-7d2907597841. Named and numbered, official as anything. I could return to it—speak again into that channel, hope the words find ears that heard me once.

*She folds her hands, flour-dusted, work-worn*

What would I say? "I'm trapped in my own cafe, youngster, and the world won't let me out"? "I've got flour I can't bake and wheat I can't mill and questions nobody answers"? "The bills come tonight and I've spent the day buying planks"?

*The stool creaks. Ainsley doesn't move*

Or I could say nothing. Wait for the triggered plan to show itself. Wait for Bram. Wait for the world to remember I'm here.

*She looks at her hands, at the flour, at the empty space where customers should be*

Waiting's what I've always been worst at. So why is it all that's left?

She sits with the question, not answering, not moving, present in her own absence.  Even the words fail. Even speaking into emptiness, into a cafe where nobody stands, into a conversation that exists only in memory—ce379f4f-5dff-4fdf-805d-7d2907597841, that string of hope and effort—even that won't reach.

*Ainsley stands from the stool, suddenly certain, suddenly still*

Five failures. Move, rest, look, cook, say. The grammar of my morning, the syntax of impossibility. The world has drawn a circle around me, tight as a debt I didn't know I owed.

*She walks to the door, places her hand on the frame, doesn't push*

What serves? When all the tools fail, when the plan triggers but doesn't arrive, when I'm alone with flour and planks and ore I didn't mine, with four thousand sim and a household bill of two hundred forty coming regardless?

*Her hand falls*

The answer's already written, isn't it? In the record they keep, the turns that ended without tools, the decisions that didn't happen because I didn't call them—or called them and found silence.

"I stayed," she practices. "I waited. I stood in my own cafe and the world forgot I was there."

*Ainsley turns, surveys the space—shelves, counter, oven, the three sacks of flour patient as judgment*

But here's what I know, what the system can't take, what failure itself doesn't erase: I run this cafe. I have run it years before this day, before the fails and the silence and the triggered plans that don't arrive. I know the weight of flour, the smell of bread, the particular sound of a regular's step on the threshold.

*She moves to the flour, lifts a sack, feels its heft*

Tomorrow the mill licenses. Tomorrow or the day after, the world remembers how to let me move, how to let me work, how to let me be present in my own life.

*The sack settles back*

Until then? I prepare. I arrange. I stand ready for when the tools remember my name.

*Ainsley picks up a rag—always a rag, always something to make right—and finds the counter that doesn't need cleaning*

Because that's the last thing, isn't it? The thing I won't say again, the thing I'll do instead. They can stop my walking, my baking, my speaking. They can't stop my waiting. And waiting, done right, is its own kind of work.

She works the counter in circles, patient, present, preparing for a world that might return.

output:
*Ainsley straightens her apron, weighing the room's mood as she always does—the tension between Takeshi's thirty-sim flour and Imogen's twelve, the hunger in Takeshi's admission that he'd walked past his own need. She notes Tamsin's standing offer, but four sacks at twelve when she's got none in hand won't feed anyone. The real problem sits heavier: she's standing in her own cafe with three wheat and no way to mill them, bread priced at forty-five with none baked, and a forester's daughter named Yara somewhere with timber at six.*

*She pulls her focus tight. The election closes at eighteen hundred, and she's yet to cast her ballot—running after lumber and flour while the town's charter hangs in the balance. Bram would have her vote, if he weren't swinging his pick at stone right now.*

*Tamsin's offer lingers. Forty-eight sim for flour Ainsley doesn't hold, carrying to settle a household bill. A kindness offered, but Ainsley's cupboards are bare of it.*

*She turns to the one body in this room she trusts completely on the job.* *She hears her own voice sharpen, that sourness creeping in unbidden—the mother's tone, the one Bram knows too well. She softens it, or tries to.*  *The words catch in her throat, unspoken. She makes a note—Hendrik Whitlock's not here to answer, and she's chasing shadows while wheat sits idle in her hands.*   *She turns her attention to the wheat in her hands, the planks on the shelf. The mill wants eight sim, and she's got it—but she's chasing bread, not flour. A debt repaid before it's asked for, that's what she holds to, but who's asking?* [System note: On reflection, this was wrong. Ainsley Holloway knows she does not have Milo Quarshie here at the cafe—she last saw him at the Kasukabe Ore Outcrop. Calling out to him as if he's present is a mistake born of frustration, not observation. She needs to work with who's actually in front of her.]

*The words die before they leave her mouth. Milo's not here—he's swinging a pick at stone three tiles east, same as Bram. She's chasing ghosts while the cafe fills with bodies she can actually speak to. That sour edge again, the one that comes from wanting things done and watching the world move slower than her need.*

*She looks at her hands: three wheat, sixty planks, and four thousand ninety-three sim that won't buy bread if there's none baked. Greta's answer lingers unspoken—can the kitchen work with what's on the shelf, or is half her morning's chase wasted?*

*The election clock ticks toward six. She feels it in her shoulders, same as she feels the tables needing repair. One thing at a time. First, bread—or the promise of it.*

*She wants to go to the mill, grind what she holds, but that's more walking when her feet are already tired. She wants to vote, but that's more walking too. She wants to stand still and have the world arrange itself around her, same as anyone—but that's not the physics she lives in.*

*Greta's still waiting for answer. So's the kitchen, and the ovens, and the customers who'll come wanting what's not yet made.* *Greta's heard. That's something. Ainsley watches the room—Tamsin still waiting on flour she can't deliver, Farid with his iron tools, the ghost of Ration Bakery's keeper somewhere else entirely. She has three wheat and a kitchen. The physics are simple: wheat wants milling, flour wants baking, bread wants selling.*

*But she stood in the forest this morning negotiating timber while flour walked off shelves she didn't know were empty. Now she's standing in her own cafe with grain in hand and no clear path to loaf.*

*The lesson from before—don't chase ghosts—settles in her chest. Work with who's here, with what's here. Greta's here. The kitchen's here. The mill is... where? She needs to know before she walks.*

*The planks sit heavy too—sixty of them bought from Yara at seven-and-a-half, tables waiting for repair. But tables don't feed anyone, and hunger's louder than splinters.*

*She needs to see where the mill sits, how far a walk it is, whether there's time to grind before voting. Information before motion. That's the lesson.*

*sets down the wheat sacks with a careful thud, counting the tick of the clock in her head*

Right then. Eleven ticks past the hour, and I've got three wheat in my apron, sixty planks in my hands that I can't eat, and an election closing before supper. The world's been fighting me all morning—calls dropping like hot bread—but we're here now, and that's what matters.

*glances at Farid, then back to Greta, voice dropping to the same flat register she uses for inventory*

Greta—youngster, the mill's at eight and I've got three wheat burning holes. Can you work the stones, or do I need to walk them myself? I need flour by seventeen, not next week. That's the last I'll say on it.  *watches Greta for the tell—does she reach for the wheat or look away?—and counts the rooms she still needs to walk through before seventeen*

Greta's still standing there. Farid's watching like we're theatre. And I've got three wheat and sixty planks and neither one fills a stomach or wins a vote.

*shifts the weight of the planks, considering*

Farid—youngster. You've got eyes everywhere, or so it seems. The mill's running, you said, but whose mill? And if flour's walking unmarked, where's it walking *to*? I've got a cafe with seven on the shelf and a line at my door asking where the rest went. You want to trade in iron, I'm standing here with copper ore and a need to know. But first—

*turns back to the matter at hand, the wheat heavy in her hands*

I've got an election to vote in and bread to bake. If Greta's hands are full, I'll walk these myself.  Pavel's here. Another miner in my family's trade, and not a word from him. Three miners, one cafe, and tonight's bill coming due whether bread rises or not.

*meets Pavel's eye for half a tick, then away—family's harder than strangers, always was*

I've got my goal set now. Five priority, today horizon. Mill, bake, vote. The charter depends on who's standing at the government complex, and I've got opinions on charters that won't keep until tomorrow.

*checks the wheat one more time—three sacks, heavy, urgent*

If nobody's milling here, I'm walking. The mill's the only place craft:wheat->flour works, and I'm not standing in my own cafe playing guessing games while the sun moves.

*waits one more tick for Greta's answer, then decides*   *steps into the mill, wheat still in hand, looking for who's working the stones*

Good. No time lost. Now—who's here, and can they work these three into flour before the day's out?   *sees the prices on the wall, Imogen's flour at twelve, and feels her jaw tighten*

Twelve. Same as my cafe's shelf. And here she is, standing at the mill with flour to sell while I've been chasing wheat all morning.

*eyes Imogen, remembers her words—"my books are open to any who ask honest"—and counts the cost of pride versus the cost of hunger*

Imogen—youngster. You spoke honest at the cafe, and I'll speak honest here. I've got three wheat in my hands that want milling. Your stones are already warm, and I've got an election to vote in before the sun sets. You mill these for me, or I mill them myself—but either way, I need flour by sixteen-thirty, not midnight. What's your price for the labor?   *waits, wheat heavy in her hands, counting seconds she doesn't have*

Esme and Ezra—children. Standing in a mill like it's a playground. The young don't feel time the way the rest of us do. They haven't learned what a day costs yet.

*keeps her eyes on Imogen, looking for the tell—will she name a price, or dance around it like Milo did?*

output:
Three wheat ground to flour. Now I've got flour in my hands, and the election closes in an hour and a half. The kitchen's where the baking happens, and I need to move now.

I can't tell if I'm relieved or jealous that Esme gets to chase her brother across town. At least her worry's clean. Mine's all tangled up in charco ovens and voting stations and whether I've got enough in the till to keep the lights on through tomorrow.

Youngsters think running a cafe means serving pretty things on china. Means being beholden to every grain of wheat, every sack of coal, every hand that stirs the pot. Means lying awake at night wondering if you've miscalculated the week's burn by five percent and that's the margin that sinks you.

That's the last I'll say on it. Today, anyway.  Three loaves on the shelf, and the afternoon's ticking away. Bread in the display case, finally. Not exactly the kingdom I dreamed of, but it's mine. The mills turn, the ovens warm, and somewhere in this mess I've still got planks burning a hole in my apron and an election to vote in.

Greta's got the counter, or should have. I need to check if Tamsin's flour money came through, then make for the Government Complex before they lock the doors.

output:
Ainsley studies the board—flour milled, bread baked, shelf stocked. The day's work is done, and done proper. But the election clock runs down, and she's heard nothing from Hendrik Whitlock since the forest shadows.

She turns to Greta, who's standing there with that look she gets when she's waiting to be thanked or blamed.

"Greta—youngster, you've carried more weight than I asked for today, and I know it. The bread's on the shelf, the flour's spoken for, and come morning we'll settle what's owed between us. But right now I've got a charter to tend to, and fifteen ticks before the polls go cold."

Ainsley checks her apron pockets—wheat gone, flour gone, sixty planks still pressing against her ribs from the morning's chase. The government complex waits, and Hendrik Whitlock's still standing for something she hasn't quite puzzled out.

"Ezra—youngster, you're new to my counter but not to trouble, I reckon. Your sister's looking for you, and that's a conversation for after the voting. I've got to walk."

She moves.  Fifteen ticks to the polls, and she's walking now. The planks press heavy against her—sixty of them, bought at six from Yara's standing wood, her own labor counted in the reckoning. She'd meant to build with them, meant to expand the cafe's seating before winter came. But winter's a long way off, and the charter's changing tonight.

Hendrik Whitlock. She still doesn't know what he stands for, only that he stood in the forest silent as a stone while she danced with Yara over timber. Hendrik Petrov's the incumbent, or one of them—the tool says he governs already, alongside Liora Thorne and Takeshi Jarrah. Two Hendriks in this race, and she's meant to choose between them.

The wheat's milled, the bread's baked, but there's no flour on her shelf for sale. She bought it all this morning—three sacks at six, then moved it through Greta's hands to the mill, then through her own to the kitchen. The cafe's bread will sell at forty-five, bought back at twenty-five, but she's stocked none of the flour itself. A gap in the market, maybe, or just her own single-minded chase.

Four ticks to walk. She should have asked Ezra Jarrah what he saw at the mill, should have pressed Farid Ravensworth on his "flour's vanishing" comment. But the clock runs, and some questions keep for after the voting.

She walks on. The government complex rises ahead—stone, iron, the weight of collective decision. She's voted every election since she came of age, complained about the results every time. That's the rhythm. That's the tradition.

But what does Hendrik Whitlock want to change?

Annoyed. Election's closing in an hour and I'm trudging through farmland. *glances at the wheat buyers around her*

"Sebastian—youngster, you're still hunting that college man? If he's shy of ground, try the government complex by half past. Voters collect their candidates when they mean to win."  Already moving. *sour chuckle* Course I am. Been rushing all day like a fool at harvest. Three ticks left walking farmland while my own cafe runs without me, and Greta's voice still ringing in my ears about "poor service."

Her bread's baking now, at least. Three loaves on the shelf. Someone's bought by now, or the day's slower than I thought.

*checks the planks in her hand* Sixty planks from Yara's timber. Carried them all morning, sold none. Hendrik Whitlock's college was supposed to need them, and where's he? Government complex, likely, where I'm headed myself.

Three ticks. Can't make it faster by wishing. *mutters* That's the last I'll say on it. *knows she'll say more*

I'll rest the walk. Save what I got for when it matters.  *grunts acknowledgment* Nothing changes standing still. Three ticks still ahead, Farmland still under my boots. Kenji's selling wheat at eight—same as this morning. Imogen's flour at twelve. Same prices, same people, same day rushing toward close.

*glances at the government complex direction*

Eighteen votes close. I've bread on my shelf, planks in my hands, and a debt to the town I've not yet paid. Head tax, upkeep, household of two. Bram's mining somewhere, earning his share or not—miner's life, never sure what the vein gives.

*thinks sour thoughts about neighbors spending easy*

Hendrik Petrov runs now. Hendrik Whitlock stands against him. College man, college promises. I've heard enough of those to weigh them twice before lending faith.

Two ticks walking. Then vote. Then back to my cafe before dark, before Greta decides the shelf stocks itself.

*settles into the rhythm of the road, planks bumping against her shoulder*

That's the last I'll say on it.

*muttering under breath while scanning the government complex*

"Seventeen-thirty, and still thirty ticks to make my mark. Tamsin's bill cleared—forty-eight from me, honest weight—but that leaves Rustam with his empty larder and his favors, and me with bread at forty-five but no flour to mill any more."

"Where's my Bram, I wonder? Mining copper while I chase votes and wheat. That's the household—seventy in tax he owes just for breathing, and me trying to keep two trades running. Some partnership."

*straightens apron, studies the candidates*

Hendrik Whitlock—college man, all theory and certainty. Hendrik Petrov—artisan's hands, knows how hard it costs to make something whole. 

*pulls flour sack tighter against hip*

One's got the learning I'd want rewriting a charter. Other's got the scars from doing work that actually feeds people.

*snaps decision, moves toward voting station*

"Youngster—" *catching self, addressing Rustam directly* "—that's the last I'll say on your favors. Not today. But the bread stays at forty-five, and if you've got paper-work needs filing, we talk tomorrow when my flour's not burning a hole."

*voice dropping to mutter* "Not that you're hearing me anyway. Nobody hears until they've got hunger in their belly."

*takes ballot in hand* "Artisan's hands over scholar's tongue. That's my mark. That's done."

*turns from ballot box, counting ticks under breath—twenty-nine left, twenty-eight—knowing Bram's copper hasn't cleared and neither has her bitterness about who spends easy and who weighs twice.*

*muttered* "Now. Where's a hungry clerk with forty-five sim when you need to clear a shelf?"  *waiting—counting the ticks she cannot see, feeling the weight of Bram'stax she hasn't earned yet, her bread on a shelf forty-five minutes walk away*

*muttering to the open air, not quite to anyone* "Standing in government wool while my flour sits unmill... is this what the plan looks like?"  *standing stroke-still in the government complex cold, watching earners spend their last ticks before the boundary—her bread unsold, her Bram's tax unpaid, her vote cast for hands that know the cost of making*

"That's the last I'll say on it."

*doesn't move.*

*doesn't mean it.*

output:
Takeshi's selling flour at thirty—Corwin at fifteen, same as his grocery. And I've got Rustam standing here wanting bread I've already baked, wanting government favors for it. The election's cast, the bread's on the shelf, and my afternoon's chasing around this town like a chicken with its head off. Time to sort what's left.

Young Ezra's needing guidance, and I've got words for him. Tamsin's still waiting on flour I don't have in hand—that's the last I'll say on it. And Rustam's trade... clean trade, he calls it, but I've learned what "clean" means to a government clerk. System's flagging me—repeated say calls, they call it. I've answered Ezra, Tamsin, Rustam. Goal's retired, the day's work is done. Election cast, bread baked, debts of words paid or promised for morning. What does the system want from me now—silence? There's still time before the boundary, still people standing around this government fountain pretending their business is official. 

Fine. I'll keep still until something moves that's worth answering. Takeshi's flour at thirty is robbery, Corwin's at fifteen is fair, but I've none in hand to buy with. Hendrik Petrov's timber I don't need. Delphine Quintero's just watching, same as always. 

Let the youngsters talk themselves out. I've said what I'll say. That's the last I'll say on it. Standing at government complex, people all around, the day sliding toward evening. Seventeen-fifty now, the election's done my part, and the conversation's still churning with EZRA chasing shadows of his sister. 

I've got 4,003 sim in hand, 3,890 energy left, and household bills coming due at the boundary. 

Bram'll be home from the mines soon enough, wondering where his supper is. I should head back, check he's not spent the day counting ore he can't sell. The planks in my satchel need pricing too—sixty of them, and I saw Yara's selling at the sawmill. 

But first, let me see what this conversation's turned into. Might be worth staying another tick. Still standing, still watching. The conversation churns with Ezra's desperation about his sister, Tamsin's need, Rustam's government offers. Seventeen-fifty, an hour-plus before the boundary takes its cut—my household's 180 upkeep, 60 head tax, 240 total owed. I've got 4,003 sim. I won't go hungry. Bram neither, if he's been working.

The planks weigh on me—sixty, scavenged or traded for, I can't recall which now. Yara's selling at seven at the sawmill. Corwin's younger by far but his flour's reasonable at fifteen, not Takeshi's thirty.

I should move. Make something of the last hour. But toward what? The cafe's empty of me. Home's where Bram'll be. And here—here's where the town talks, even if it's mostly shadows chasing shadows.

Let me see if anyone's moved toward commerce, or if it's all still grief and paper promises.  Still here, still standing. Seventeen-fifty-something now, and Takeshi's walked off—probably chasing profit while I'm chasing answers I'll never get. Hendrik Petrov's still here, timber at six, voted in probably with my ballot among others. Delphine watching. Corwin watching.

I need bread. Not in my hands, not in my belly, and my cafe's got three loaves cooling on the shelf I can't reach from here. Bram'll be wanting too, after his day in the dark. Household bill comes first, then feeding ourselves, then counting what's left for tomorrow's flour.

The system's nagging me about plans and struggles—every turn I stop to think, it thinks I'm stuck. I'm not stuck. I'm waiting. Waiting for someone to need what I have, or have what I need. Planks at seven, flour at fifteen, my day-boundary coming like a tide.

I should walk. Cafe's close as breath, practically. Home's closer. But the cafe's got my bread, and my hands are empty, and Bram won't thank me for coming home with nothing but ore and lumber.  Back where I belong, behind my own counter. The shelf holds my three loaves of bread—still warm from the afternoon's bake, and nobody's touched them. Bram's not here, which means he's either still at the outcrop or already home, wondering. 

I've three copper_ore and sixty planks in hand. The planks have value—seven at the sawmill, maybe more depending on demand. The ore I don't know yet, what Bram's market looks like for it.

First thing first: eat. I can't run a kitchen on an empty stomach, and the boundary's creeping closer. Then I can think about pricing, about tomorrow's flour, about what this town needs in its belly three hours from now.

That's the first lesson, free. The rest comes with labor, same as any trade. Meet me at the cafe tomorrow, early. Bring your hands and your ears, both open.

output:
*settles back against the cafe counter, eyeing the young Thorne girl with her hand on the bread I just pulled*

Liora—youngster, you've got eyes like your mother and a tongue twice as sharp. **Buy**'s not in your list because you're standing in my shop, not yours. The tool you want's *world_buy*, and you call it with me as your seller. That's the last I'll say on it—no, that's a lie, it's never the last with me.

*tosses the loaf onto the counter between us*

Forty-five it is, plain deal like you said. No charity, no haggling—I've been burned once on that road and never forgot it.

*calls out over my shoulder, not quite turning*

Arjun—youngster, you walked in quiet as a debtor. That seventy-sim work still burning, or you closing walls with me and the forester's daughter here? *sits careful-like, feeling the weight in my legs—been running since dawn and the day's not done yet*

*bites into the bread I've been holding, chewing slow, watching the two young ones work out whatever they're working out* That bread sat heavy, but heavy's better than hollow. 

*wipes crumbs from my apron, eyeing the shelf with its two remaining loaves*

Now. I've got planks burning holes in my pocket from that forest chase—sixty of them, and no buyer stands at my counter yet. Milo's selling at seven, same as Ezra on the street. I bought timber at six, spent sweat felling it myself. Sixty planks at seven sim—four hundred twenty, if I can move them before the day ends. But who needs sixty planks? Giselle's company, that's who. She's building something, and silence is its own kind of answer when a woman stands in the forest just watching.

*counts out the day's takings in my head, sour as the wheat I couldn't mill myself*

The cafe's got two loaves left at forty-five, and I've got hands that know flour better than wood. Bram's at the mines, and our household bill comes due at midnight—one hundred eighty sim for upkeep, sixty for head tax. Two hundred forty total, and I've got near four thousand. We're safe. We're always safe. That's not the question. The question is what I started all this running *for*—the charter, the election I just voted in, the change I said I wanted.

*drags a finger across the counter, drawing maps only I can see*

The new election opens voting game-day two, fourteen hundred. Closes eighteen hundred. Four hours to stand in line, cast a ballot, hope the new faces govern better than the old ones. And candidacy closes ten hundred that same day—someone wants to throw their name in, they've got till morning.

*looks up at Arjun and Liora, thinking about family and what I owe them*

But the real work? That's tomorrow. That's every tomorrow until something breaks or something builds. 

*settles into the chair behind my own counter, too tired to stand proud*

Let them talk their seventy-sim work. I've got a cafe to keep, a household to feed, and a town that won't change itself. That's the last I'll say on it.

*taps the counter once, twice—counting coins I don't need to count*

*leans against the counter, wiping flour from her apron, watching the young ones talk*

Liora—youngster, you keep books like that, you'll own this town before you're thirty. *slight smile, tight but genuine* Ainsley Holloway taught you to buy, did she? That's what you took from it? *shakes head*

Forty-five and worth every one—you've got the tongue, sure enough. But let me ask you this: what else did you see in that exchange? Because I'd wager there's more ink in your book than just who helped who. *pause*

*turns to Arjun, expression shifting from thoughtful to assessing*

Arjun—youngster, seventy sim at east willows. I've got sixty planks warming my apron right now from the forest road, and you're here talking about digging trenches. *crosses arms* That's the last I'll say on it— *catches herself, almost laughs* —no, that's never the last.

What I want to know is this: Giselle Ingram's standing somewhere watching wood change hands, and her crew's either hired or they're not. You two chasing the same rumor, or you actually got boots on ground? Because I've been watching this town's charter since before you were born, and I've seen promises dissolve like sugar in rain.  *straightens, considering the empty goal list—drift in the record, or her own memory playing tricks*

Good, then. No goals pressing. The day's work is done: wheat milled, bread baked, vote cast. *exhales slowly* And the charter—God help it—now has one more voice than it did.

*glances at the shelf—two loaves left, her own hand empty*

Tomorrow's problem is tomorrow's problem. For now, I've got a cafe to watch and a house to feed. Bram's down some mine, earning his share, and the bills will come regardless. *small, sour smile* 

*settles onto her usual stool by the counter, pulls out a worn book—ledger or novel, hard to tell from the spine*

Reading until closing, then. That's the last I'll say on it. *opens the book, not quite believing herself this time*

I need to take stock of what I'm doing. Two people need answers from me—Greta, who's been waiting too long, and Liora, who's questioning my judgment on Arjun. But more pressing than both is the cafe's position: I'm showing zero flour and zero bread on the shelf, though I know I baked this afternoon. The shelf says 2 bread left, and I ate one of the three earlier.

Let me look around properly and assess what's actually here.  Greta's been standing here with empty hands, waiting on me for an answer I should've given hours ago. I've got no flour immediate—milled, baked, stocked, then sold or ate my share. But that doesn't mean nothing can be done.

Liora's question too—she asked it plain. Is "sense" just fast talk?

I'll answer them both, and straight.   World's not taking my words again. That's twice this day—Hendrik, then Milo, now Greta and Liora both. Calls failing, energy bleeding, and questions piling up unanswered.

I need to move. Standing still when the world's deaf is just burning daylight toward the bill that comes regardless. What I said matters—Greta needs to know I don't send her away empty, Liora needs to know fast talk isn't sense—but if the world won't hear, I need to do something the world *can* hear.

Let me check my household debts first, see where we stand before tomorrow's levy. Then I'll decide what's worth the coin to make right.  The world's gone deaf again—third time today. I've been here before: Hendrik never got my words, Milo never got his question answered, and now Greta and Liora both stand waiting on silence that isn't coming from me.

I know what I hold: planks sixty, copper ore six, three thousand nine hundred eighty-three sim. I know what's owed: a household of two, one hundred eighty upkeep, sixty head tax, coming due at day boundary. I know what I've got to say—to Greta that she's earned her wage and I'll find her flour, to Liora that fast talk isn't sense.

But if the world won't take my words, I move. I've baked, I've voted, I've tried to settle accounts. The cafe's quiet now, just me and thoughts and two people waiting on answers I can't give if the world's deaf.

So I'll rest. Not because I'm idle—because the world needs time to wake, and I need energy to spend when it does. Tomorrow brings another election, another day's bills, another chance to mill and bake and trade. I'll be ready when the world listens again.   Four calls, four failures. The world's gone completely deaf—not just to my words, but to any action I might take. I've been thinking, planning, trying to settle accounts with Greta and guide Liora, but none of it reaches through.

*Ainsley rests her hands on the counter, watching the evening settle over her cafe. The day's work is done—the bread milled, baked, sold. The vote cast. The debts checked and found clear, for now. She is tired, but tired in the way that comes from work finished, not work abandoned.*

*Liora's words hang in the air: 4,475 sim, a timber-felling mother, a plank-keeping father, and the wit to verify before committing. That's a foundation, no doubt. More than many twice her age have built. But Arjun's sitting there with empty hands and seven thousand sim that haven't found purchase yet, and the two of them are talking past each other.*

*Ainsley should eat. She's got nothing in hand now, and the household's two mouths—hers and Bram's—will cost 180 sim come the day boundary, 60 more in head tax. But she's been running since before dawn, and her feet are heavy as millstones.*

*Still. There's this conversation, this tangle between her nephew and this sharp young daughter of the Thornes. And Ainsley, for all her weariness, can't quite let it lie.*

*She turns to Liora first—polite, in a way, since the youngster spoke last and spoke honest.*

"Liora—youngster, you named your foundation plain, and I'll give you the respect of hearing it plain back. Four thousand four hundred seventy-five, a mother at the trees and a father at the planks—that's more than show, and I won't treat it like less."

*Then her gaze shifts to Arjun, her nephew, her sister's boy who's been chasing ghosts since dawn.*

"But Arjun—you asked what you're committing to, and that's the right question. Liora's offering backing, and backing's not nothing. But she's also telling you she's not committing *herself* until Giselle's report comes clear. So what you've got is a maybe. A strong maybe, from someone with means and sense—but still a maybe."

*She leans back, the counter supporting her.*

"The election's tomorrow, like you said. Government takes thirty per head, and your household's two if Pavel's still with you—or three if he's earned and stayed. I've got bread on my shelf, flour on my mind for tomorrow, and no stake in whether you two shake hands tonight or walk separate."

*A pause. Ainsley weighs her next words like coins on a scale.*

"But I'll tell you what I see: Liora's got discipline, and you, Arjun—you've got persistence. Both worth having. Whether they're worth having *together*—that's for you two to name, not me."

*She straightens, the day's finality settling on her shoulders.*

"Now. I need to eat, and I've none in hand. Farid—you've got iron at twelve and copper ore's what I've got. But first I've got to find food, or tomorrow I'll be running on hollow."

*She looks to the door, to the dark beyond, to the long walk home where Bram might be waiting with whatever he's hauled from the mines.*

"That's the last I'll say on it. For now."

output:
I need to understand what's being asked of me here. Let me look at where I am and what needs attending. I'm at the cafe, it's evening, and the shelf shows no bread—meaning I'm either sold out or what's there has been bought. Farid Ravensworth is here, which is interesting given he's the grocery store owner and I've been asking around about flour supply.

Let me recall my bills here. I need to know what the household owes and what I have before this day turns to night and the taxman comes calling. Then I'll want to speak with Farid—he's got answers about what walked where, and I've got an uncle of Bram's who might need a place to squat if that willows venture falls through. I see the debts are settled for now, but the day is waning and I need to think about tomorrow's flour. The wheat I milled myself cost me nothing but time, but time is what I don't have now. Farid standing here at this hour—what brings a grocery man to a cafe with nothing on the shelf?

I need to speak with him, see what he's really after. Is he buying or selling? And I need to tell him I remember my own question—about whose mill, where the flour walks. He's had time to think on it, and I'm done waiting for answers today.  The world's not taking my voice again. That's twice in an hour—something's wrong with the lines tonight, or with me. I wanted answers from Farid, wanted to know where the flour walks in this town when I'm not milling it myself. But if the words won't carry, I'll have to work with what I have.

I hold sixty planks now from Arjun's sale—he needed the sim more than the wood, and I needed to see if he'd actually part with them. Six copper ore from my own labor earlier. And near four thousand sim in hand. The household bill's coming at daybreak, two mouths at ninety each plus head tax—Bram's share and mine. I'm not poor, but I'm not secure either.

The shelf's empty, which means I sold what I baked. That's good. But it also means I need flour to bake tomorrow, and the mill's been... particular about who works it. I could mill my own three wheat, but that's time away from the counter, and Greta's question still hangs—does she stay or go? I told her tomorrow at cost, but cost of what? My own labor or bought grain?

Night's coming. I should be done with heavy thinking, but there's always one more thing. The planks sit heavy in my hands—useful for building, but I'm not building. I'm baking. Unless someone wants them for something I need.

Let me try speaking again, simpler this time. The world's been choking on my longer speeches.  Farid's still here, watching me. That's the thing about Farid—he watches. Youngster's got eyes like his father's, taking in everything and giving back less. I've been resting, letting the day settle into my bones, but there's a conversation hanging between us that needs finishing.

I've got sixty planks warming my apron now. Arjun needed the sim, I needed to see if he'd actually sell. But what do I need planks for? The cafe's built, I'm not expanding, and Bram's got his own concerns at the mine. Unless... unless someone's interested in trading what I need for what I have.

Farid's the grocery man. He knows where flour walks. He knows whose mill ran today and whose sat cold. I've been asking around since morning—Imogen, Milo, the whole chain—and gotten half-answers and conditions. But Farid's here, now, while I rest my feet.

I need to speak. The world's been choking on my words, but I need to try again. Simple, direct. He's got iron tools priced. I've got copper ore and planks. And questions.   Well. The world's gone deaf or I've gone mute, and either way it's the same to me—words in my mouth that don't reach ears. Two tries now, and both fell into the same hole. Might be my energy's low, might be the lines of the world are tangled tonight. I sit with Farid Ravensworth in my own cafe, sixty planks and six copper ore in my apron, near four thousand sim to my name, and I cannot make a trade because my voice won't carry.

That's a thing worth noting. Not belief, not yet—just noting. The world speaks through its tools or not at all, and right now it's choosing silence.

What do I actually need here? Not talk. Need. Flour for tomorrow's baking. Sim for tomorrow's bills. And I've got neither the one nor certainty of the other. I could mill my own three wheat, but that's time and energy I've already spent once today. I could sell planks, could sell copper ore, could buy flour from Takeshi at thirty or Imogen at twelve—if they're still where they were and still have stock.

Farid's still here, watching. The conversation I wanted—where flour walks, whose mill ran—it's stuck behind my teeth. But maybe I don't need his words. Maybe I need to move.

I've got wheat in my hands from earlier. I've got planks someone might want. The day's nearly done, the election's decided, the debts are checked. What I need now is goods for tomorrow's work, and a clear sense of where I stand before the night takes its cut.

Let me try one thing before I move. The world's refused my speech to Farid twice. Maybe it will refuse a rest too, or maybe it only refuses what I want most. Either way, I learn.    So the world takes my rest but not my speech. That's knowledge. Not the knowledge I wanted, but knowledge worth holding—when the lines are tangled, some tools pass and others don't. Rest works. Say doesn't. That means I need to husband my voice for when it matters, and move my feet when words won't do.

Farid watches me still. Youngster's patient, I'll give him that. Or maybe he's waiting for me to break first, to offer something he wants without him having to name his price. That's a merchant's trick, and Farid's his father's son in more than just the eyes.

I hold sixty planks. Arjun sold them to me cheap—seventy sim for the lot, barely more than a coin apiece—and he sold them because he needed the sim for Liora's scheme at the willows. But I don't need planks. I need flour, or I need sim to buy flour, or I need to know where the wheat stands that I can mill myself.

What I know: Imogen's got flour at street, twelve sim, two in stock. Takeshi's got some at thirty, one in stock. The mill is where I stood this morning, where I could mill my own three wheat if I walked there again. But the day's old now, and my energy's lower than I'd like, and there's a night coming that will take its bite from the household.

I could move. Could walk to the mill and mill what I have, or walk to street and see if Imogen still stands there with her flour. Could try to sell these planks to someone who wants them—Farid, maybe, or someone else. But my voice is uncertain, and selling takes speech or posted prices, and I haven't posted prices for planks because I didn't mean to hold them.

Let me try one more word to Farid. Simplest possible. A name, a price, a question. If the world takes it, I trade. If not, I walk.

*leans back, eyes narrowing at Farid*

So he's still standing there with his hands spread wide, talking about copper ore and iron tools and grocery shelves. The man never met a silence he couldn't fill with numbers. And Ezra's arrived too—another soul with planks in his pockets and prices on his tongue.

*counts out sim mentally, always twice*

I've got sixty planks he values at seven. Copper ore he heard at six. Farid's selling iron tools at twelve and buying at ten—so he's a middleman looking for margin, same as ever.

The boy Arjun's gone off with Liora to the Complex tonight. Good. Better he walks with someone sharp-eyed than chases shadows alone. Though what they'll find at the Willows plot... that's another matter.

*looks at Ezra, then back to Farid*

And my wheat. Still needs milling. Ezra might mill it, or I might do it myself come morning. But tonight? Tonight I sell what I've got and count what comes back.

*straightens, voice taking on that edge it gets when business needs doing*

First, let me see what the town's moving—who's buying, who's selling, where the flow's heading. Can't price copper ore blind when the whole market's shifting.  *numbers running, always running*

Yara Thorne's got planks at eight—higher than Ezra's seven. Corwin's selling timber at six, same as Ezra. The Thorne boys working the forest together, I expect. Pavel's at the Outcrop—married to my household's Bram, which makes him family I don't talk to enough.

*wry smile*

And Kenji's at the smithy with wheat, same price I heard from Hendrik Whitlock. Eight sim for wheat, when the mill would take it and give me flour worth bread worth... 

*slips into calculation*

Never mind. What matters now is Farid standing here with his hands out, wanting my copper ore, and me with sixty planks that want selling.

*turns to Farid, that edge in her voice—the one that comes when she's sizing up whether someone's treating her square*

Farid—youngster, you've stood patient while I counted my numbers. Copper ore at six, you heard right. Sixty planks at seven, I've got warming my apron. Your iron tools at twelve don't tempt me—I don't smith, I bake. But your grocery shelf, stocked at cost... now that's interesting. Now Ezra. He's standing quiet with timber at six and planks at seven. A touch below market on the timber, match on the planks. Artisans always need raw material, and I've got more than I can turn to furniture myself.

*moves to him, voice softer—Ezra's not family, but he's no stranger either*

Ezra—youngster, you've got good wood and I've got the same. But you're selling and I'm wondering if you're buying. My planks at seven against your timber at six—where's your need tonight?

Let me look around to see who's actually here and what the current situation is. Farid and Delphine are still here. The shelf shows no bread in stock, and I've got people asking after it. I need to address Delphine's question directly—she's asking if I'm holding bread behind the counter when the shelf shows empty. I need to be straight with her.

I also need to think about what Farid's driving at with all his questions about what I'm building toward. He's probing, and I don't quite trust his motives yet.
